questions.q: In a qubit connectivity graph, what does an edge between two nodes represent?
options: That a direct two-qubit gate can be applied between those two physical qubits with no intermediate steps
That the two qubits have identical coherence times
That the two qubits are physically touching on the chip
That the two qubits were manufactured in the same fabrication batch
questions.explain: The connectivity graph's edges mark exactly which pairs of physical qubits support a direct two-qubit gate -- it's a statement about the hardware's physical coupling, not about proximity, manufacturing, or coherence.

questions.q: Why did IBM choose the sparser heavy-hex lattice for its superconducting chips instead of a denser grid layout?
options: Heavy-hex eliminates the need for a dilution refrigerator
Heavy-hex was chosen purely for aesthetic/marketing reasons with no engineering tradeoff
Heavy-hex uses fewer qubits overall than a grid layout
Heavy-hex reduces the frequency-collision problem that arises when densely packed qubits have near-identical resonant frequencies and interfere with each other
questions.explain: Heavy-hex trades some connectivity for fewer frequency collisions between physically close qubits -- a deliberate engineering tradeoff, not an arbitrary or cosmetic choice.

questions.q: Why can't a superconducting chip simply wire every qubit to every other qubit and avoid connectivity limits entirely?
options: It's a software limitation imposed by the compiler, unrelated to the physical chip
All-to-all wiring is possible and routinely done on superconducting chips today
Superconducting qubits are physically incapable of being coupled to more than one neighbor under any circumstances

The number of required couplers and control lines scales roughly with the square of the qubit count, running into real limits on chip space, line routing off the cooled chip, and crosstalk from extra coupling elements
questions.explain: Full wiring scales roughly quadratically with qubit count and runs into real fabrication, line-routing, and crosstalk constraints -- the sparse connectivity graph reflects genuine physical limits, not an arbitrary restriction.

questions.q: What makes a single trapped-ion chain's connectivity graph different from a superconducting chip's?
options: Trapped-ion connectivity graphs are always heavy-hex, same as superconducting chips
Trapped-ion chains have no connectivity graph because they use lasers instead of wires
Trapped-ion chains always have fewer qubits than superconducting chips, so the graph is smaller but the same shape
Because every ion shares the chain's collective motional modes, the graph is effectively all-to-all rather than nearest-neighbor
questions.explain: Because ions in one trap share motional modes rather than fixed point-to-point wiring, any ion can be coupled to any other ion in the same chain -- an all-to-all graph, unlike a superconducting chip's fixed sparse wiring.

questions.q: Why is checking a device's connectivity graph a useful first step before designing or compiling a circuit for it?
options: Connectivity graphs are identical across all hardware vendors, so checking it provides no new information
It replaces the need to know a device's gate error rates entirely
It is only useful after a circuit has already failed to run on real hardware
It immediately shows which logical qubit pairs can interact directly and which pairs will require extra routing help, before any compilation work begins
questions.explain: The connectivity graph tells you up front which qubit pairs are 'free' to interact and which aren't, which is exactly the information the next lessons build on for circuit design and SWAP-based routing.
